result.reason: The passage directly discusses the Gemara's answer invoking Shmuel's interpretation of b'omdin al basisam, which is precisely what the 'Pieces on Pedestals' section's prose describes.

The passage states the core dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about whether an idol that breaks by itself is prohibited or permitted — this is the foundational disagreement that 'Rabba's Gezeirah' section directly builds upon as Reish Lakish's position that Rabba's gezeirah must defend.

The entire 33-item passage covers the continuous dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about a spontaneously broken idol, and while items 28-29 specifically match the 'Shaving the Idol' prose of heading 0, that heading is the earliest candidate and the full passage (items 1-33) belongs together under one heading rather than split across multiple sections.

The passage shows Rabbi Yochanan raising an objection (eitivei) to Reish Lakish using Rabbi Yosei's ruling about vegetables under an asheira, asking why the fallen leaves aren't treated like an idol that broke on its own — this is Rabbi Yochanan challenging Reish Lakish, not Reish Lakish challenging Rabbi Yochanan, matching heading 0's description of Rabbi Yochanan asking 'tehavi k'avodat kochavim shenishbeira me'aleha' and Reish Lakish responding with the same gezeirah; heading 1's prose incorrectly frames this as Reish Lakish challenging Rabbi Yochanan.

All three items form the continuous chain of question-answer-objection-resolution about falling leaves from an asheira tree: item 1 is Rabbi Yochanan's answer (ikar avodah zarah kayemet), item 2 is the pushback from shavings, and item 3 is Rav Huna's resolution — all of which the 'Falling Leaves' prose describes precisely, whereas the 'Natural Growth Rule' prose describes items 2 and 3 but not item 1, meaning the passage starts under 'Falling Leaves'.

Both items present Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan using the nest case — item 1 is the mishna/baraita he cites and item 2 is the initial analysis assuming the bird broke branches from the asheira tree — which precisely matches the 'Nests on Trees' prose describing Reish Lakish's challenge and his argument that material breaking off from avodah zarah on its own becomes mutar.

All three items discuss the Gemara's explanation that the bird brought branches from elsewhere (de'aytei etzim me'alma), and the proof from the hekdesh case (lo nehenin velo mo'alin) that the twigs must be external — exactly what the 'Chicks Not Twigs' prose describes in detail.

All three items discuss the same ongoing Gemara discussion about the hekdesh tree nest case — the gidulin principle, Rabbi Abbahu's interpretation of 'yattiz' regarding chicks, and Rabbi Ya'akov's/Rav Ashi's distinctions between eggs and chicks — all of which are explicitly addressed in the 'Eggs & Young Birds' prose.

The passage is the mishnah itself about finding vessels with sun/moon/dragon images and casting them into the Dead Sea, which is precisely what the 'Destroying Vessels' section's prose introduces and discusses.

Both items — the Gemara's contradiction from the baraita listing many objects of worship, and Abaye's resolution distinguishing 'worship anything found' from 'craft only the three important ones for decoration' — are precisely what the 'Create vs. Find' prose describes, making that the correct placement.
The passage is Rav Sheshet's consolidation of the baraitot into three rules about permitted/prohibited images, which is precisely what the prose under heading 0 ('Rav Sheshet's Rules') describes.

The passage presents the Gemara's challenge to the 'making' interpretation of Rav Sheshet's ruling, citing the verse about not making images of God's celestial attendants — precisely what the 'Making Idols Problem' prose describes.
